results.text:
Talk about making love before you do it

From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.

Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.

Most couples don’t talk honestly about sex until they’re already having it. Bad timing. Once I’m naked with someone, saying what I actually want can suddenly mean interrupting the whole thing or disappointing her. I’d rather have that conversation earlier, while neither of us is trying to keep a moment going.

I don’t expect either of us to know everything already. I may not know what I want yet; she may not either. “I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you” is a perfectly good answer. Still, there are things I’d rather find out by talking than by guessing: what helps her body relax and open, what just doesn’t work, whether there’s anything kinky she needs to be able to say, and whether her past has made her want or avoid certain things. She should know the same about me.

We may even be using sex for different things. One of us may be feeling bonding while the other is feeling play. Another time it may feel sacred, or just be how we come down from a bad day.

And sooner or later our sex drives probably won’t match. One of us will want more, less, or something different. We can’t solve that in advance. I’d just rather make it normal to say so before the mismatch turns into quiet resentment.

Then comes the harder version of the same conversation: we’re naked and one of us thinks the truth will disappoint the other. Can we still say it? Bodies fitting isn’t enough.

Can Casual Sex or a Situationship Actually Be Honest?

Your body doesn’t know that you picked someone up at a bar and agreed it was only for fun. Oxytocin, vasopressin, and the rest can start attaching you anyway. Then the next morning, you’re wondering why they didn’t call. Well, not getting pulled in any further is the best outcome still available, actually, since you just played Russian Roulette with a potential life bond to a stranger.

results.text:
What are you actually choosing together?

A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? I can hear a whole future in those two words—sex, exclusivity, living together, money, children, caregiving—while she may only mean that we really like each other and want to see what happens. Sometimes I like letting a relationship flow without naming every part. I just don’t want us to discover later that we were silently agreeing to different things.

One honest option is basically a “practical partnership.” Two people may share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, and maybe have sex without pretending the whole thing rests on overwhelming romantic love. That feels wrong to me because I’ve been in love, but I don’t think there’s anything inherently wrong with it if both people know that’s what they’re doing. What would scare me is one of them meeting a heartthrob at work or church one day and suddenly wondering why they settled for less.

Another honest option is a romance with humility, even if romance and humility seem to clash. Two people really are in love and want to build something together. They can choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life without pretending they can guarantee what either heart will feel ten years later.

My actual ideal is to have intimacy embedded in community. Obviously most people are not going to live in a free-love community unless we really have a New Earth soon. But, as Pema Chodron says to prisoners when teaching them meditation, “Start Where You Are.” Build mutual friendships, and keep other sources of meaning and support alive.

Then the questions change for me. If the romance changes, which parts are still supposed to remain? Are we promising actions, or quietly pretending to promise permanent feelings? Which needs are we still going to meet outside the relationship?

And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? What counts as betrayal, and what just means we need a serious conversation? If our lives change, can we revisit the agreement honestly? If we separate, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe any children involved?

These are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with! You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there's real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity.
